segments.text: Your season-end basketball tournament starts next week, so you decide to brush up on the rules.
You upload your league's massive 200-page rulebook and ask the AI how many fouls until I'm out of the game.
The system answers immediately, five fouls and you foul out.
But wait a second, you remember a player picking up five fouls in last year's tournament and staying in.
You dig into the pages yourself and find a special section near the end.
Regular season games have a five foul limit, but in tournament games players get six.
The AI didn't make up the five foul limit, it pulled the standard rule exactly as written.
What it gave you was an incomplete answer because it missed the exception buried later in the text.
This is the document trap.
We assume that uploading a file means the AI has read every single word.
To understand why it hasn't, we need to look at how these systems actually process long texts.
An AI can only answer from the exact text that reaches its context window.
A short file fits in there perfectly, but a massive stack of paper hits a memory limit,
forcing the system to hunt for the parts that seem most relevant.
This flowchart shows the common three-step process AI uses to handle those massive files.
First is split.
The system breaks the long document down into smaller, manageable pieces.
Next is search.
The AI scans those pieces, looking for keywords and overall meaning that match your question.
Finally, load.
The system takes those selected pieces and puts them into the context window to generate your answer.
Notice the banner at the bottom.
The search step acts as a strict gatekeeper.
It completely decides which parts of the document reach the final answer.
This is exactly how the basketball mistake happened.
The search mechanism scanned the pieces, found the regular season foul rule right away,
filled its context window, and left the tournament exception out completely.
The technical term for this sequence is retrieval augmented generation, or RAG.
The system retrieved passages from your rulebook to augment its generated answer.
When retrieval grabs the right passages, the AI gives you a perfect summary.
When retrieval leaves something behind, the AI leaves you vulnerable to costly errors.
To stop this from happening, we can use a framework of four specific moves to guide the retrieval process.
Move one, name the section.
If you use the document's exact headings, you give the search process a highly specific target.
Move two, ask one thing.
Asking a single, focused question keeps the retrieval step from splitting at the tension.
Let's apply those two to our rulebook.
Instead of a general question, tell the AI to look directly in the tournament section
and ask only about the personal foul limit.
If the answer still misses the mark, use move three, share what matters.
Bypass the search entirely by manually pasting or uploading just the relevant pages.
Signally, move four, ask for the quote.
Instruct the AI to quote the exact passage it used to form its response.
The ultimate goal of all four moves is simply to make the correct passages easier to find.
Forcing a quotation is crucial.
It isn't because the AI is flawless at quoting, but because having the text right there in the chat
allows you to verify its claim against the original book.
You guarantee accuracy by treating the AI like a search engine that needs targeted keywords
rather than a human who has read the whole file cover to cover.
This trap applies to situations with much higher stakes than a weekend basketball tournament.
Apartment leases, employment contracts, and lengthy insurance policies
often contain specific conditions or exceptions buried deep within the text
that completely change how the document applies to you.
Uploading a large document is still an excellent starting point to help you process information,
provided you stay vigilant about how it works.
Remember, a missing passage can change the answer.
Ask for the passage, then check it.
